sections.title: Foreword

summary.text: The foreword by the WHO Director-General argues that technology has always driven health gains and lists digital advances from point-of-care testing to artificial intelligence. It stresses that countries should be guided by evidence rather than new gadgets and presents this as WHO's first guideline on digital interventions.

sections.extract: Human health has only ever improved because of advances in technology. From the development of modern sanitation to the advent of penicillin, anesthesia, vaccines and magnetic resonance imaging, science, research and technology have always been key drivers of better health. sections.title: Executive summary

summary.text: The executive summary explains the terms digital health, eHealth and mHealth and the 2018 World Health Assembly resolution, and warns against rolling out digital tools without evidence. It uses an adapted Tanahashi framework to link digital interventions to health system gaps in accountability, supply, demand, quality and affordability. It sets out the guideline's aims and stresses that digital tools do not replace functioning health systems. The end shows how ten recommendations, from birth and death notification to telemedicine, decision support and training content, fit across the health system.

sections.extract: Background Digital health, or the use of digital technologies for health, has become a salient field of practice for employing routine and innovative forms of information and communications technology (ICT) to address health needs. The term digital health is rooted in eHealth, which is defined as “the use of information and communications technology in support of health and health-related fields”. Mobile health

sections.title: Background

summary.text: The background defines digital health, eHealth and mHealth and notes over a thousand recorded digital health deployments since 2008. It recalls the 2018 Assembly resolution and warns that many tools are rolled out without evidence of benefit, so their effects must be evaluated.

sections.extract: Background Digital health, or the use of digital technologies for health, has become a salient field of practice for employing routine and innovative forms of information and communications technology (ICT) to address health needs. The term digital health is rooted in eHealth, which is defined as “the use of information and communications technology in support of health and health-related fields” (1). Mobile health

sections.title: and universal health coverage

summary.text: Explains how digital health relates to universal health coverage using an adapted Tanahashi framework. It describes performance layers for accountability, supply, demand, quality and affordability where gaps reduce coverage. It ends with a figure showing how digital interventions, applications and health content make up digital health implementations.

sections.extract: UHC aims to ensure the quality, accessibility and affordability of health services. However, shortfalls remain in ensuring access to all who need health services and in ensuring that they are delivered with the intended quality without causing financial hardship to the people accessing them (9). The Tanahashi framework published by WHO in 1978 provides a time-tested model of understanding health system performance

sections.title: Objectives of this guideline

summary.text: States that the guideline responds to the 2018 Assembly resolution by evaluating evidence on digital health interventions, including benefits, harms, feasibility and equity. It stresses that digital tools complement but do not replace core health system components, and lists the interventions reviewed, from birth notification to training content for health workers.

sections.extract: Objectives of this guideline This guideline responds to the 2018 World Health Assembly Resolution on Digital Health, requesting WHO to provide Member States with normative guidance to inform the adoption of evidence-based digital health interventions. Within the Resolution, Member States specifically request: … that WHO builds on its strengths, by developing guidance for digital health, including, but not limited

sections.title: Target audience

summary.text: Names ministry of health decision-makers and public health practitioners as the main audience, with development partners also served, and notes that recommended interventions can be used on any digital device.

sections.extract: Target audience The primary target audience for this guideline is decision-makers in ministries of health and public health practitioners, to aid them to develop a better understanding of which digital health interventions have an evidence base to address health system needs. This guideline may also prove beneficial to organizations that invest resources into digital health systems as implementation and development

sections.title: Linkages with other WHO resources

summary.text: Explains that WHO has not yet issued guidelines on which digital interventions have evidence behind them, though some clinical guidelines include digital tools. It describes related WHO resources such as the National eHealth Strategy Toolkit, the Global Observatory for eHealth, the classification of digital interventions, the Digital Health Atlas and Be He@lthy, Be Mobile.

sections.extract: Linkages with other WHO resources WHO has published several resources on digital health, yet to date has not released normative guidelines detailing recommendations about which digital health interventions are supported by demonstrable evidence for addressing specific health system challenges. Several WHO clinical and public health guidelines have been developed that include recommendations for digital technologies

sections.title: Context and the enabling environment

summary.text: Explains that the maturity of the enabling and ICT environments strongly influences how relevant and effective the recommended digital interventions will be, defining both terms. It advises assessing ecosystem readiness and, where it is weak, strengthening the health system and the enabling environment before implementation.

sections.extract: Context and the enabling environment The maturity of the ecosystem, comprising the enabling and ICT environments, has a critical influence on the relevance and impact of the recommended digital health interventions. The enabling environment is defined as the attitudes, actions, policies and practices that support the effective and efficient functioning of organizations and programmes. For digital health, this

sections.title: Linkages to broader digital health architecture

summary.text: Stresses that digital health interventions should fit into a wider digital health architecture so that systems work together rather than as isolated duplicates. It points stakeholders to complementary guidance, such as the WHO/ITU National eHealth Strategy Toolkit and the ITU Digital Health Platform Handbook, and lists related networks and communities of practice.

sections.extract: architecture Digital health interventions are intended to integrate with and fit into an overall digital health architecture. The digital health architecture provides an overview or blueprint to describe how different digital applications (software and ICT systems) and related functionalities would interact with each other within a given context (25). sections.title: Living guidelines approach

summary.text: Describes the "living guidelines" approach, under which the guideline covers a prioritised subset of mobile-accessible digital health interventions and will add further interventions and health areas as evidence emerges. It gives targeted client communication for noncommunicable diseases as an example of a planned extension.

sections.extract: Living guidelines approach This guideline includes recommendations on a list of prioritized digital health interventions accessible via mobile devices, representing a subset of a much larger set of digital interventions. This guideline aims to incorporate a broader set of emerging digital health interventions gradually in subsequent versions. The WHO Classification of digital health interventions v1.0 (13), provides

sections.title: Methods

summary.text: Outlines how the guideline was developed under the WHO handbook for guideline development, through two online surveys and three in-person meetings held between 2016 and 2018.

sections.extract: The development of this guideline followed the methods described in the second edition of the WHO handbook for guideline development (35). This institution-wide process at WHO entailed the identification of critical questions and outcomes, retrieval of the evidence, assessment and synthesis of that evidence, the formulation of recommendations, and planning for the implementation, dissemination, impact evaluation and

sections.title: Identification of priority questions

summary.text: Describes how priority questions were identified, starting from a 2016 advisory meeting that used the WHO Classification of digital health interventions and framed questions in PICO format. It explains how the questions were refined through virtual and scoping meetings and online surveys that rated outcomes, with over 300 respondents across WHO regions.

sections.extract: Identification of priority questions Process for defining the scope of interventions and outcomes The initial advisory meeting in February 2016 was used to explore the strategic direction of this guideline, including defining the objectives and the framing of digital health interventions. Since there were no preceding WHO guidelines with defined terminologies for specific digital health interventions, this meeting

sections.title: Scoping of interventions and outcomes

summary.text: Lists the digital health interventions prioritised for evidence review, including birth and death notification, stock management, client-to-provider and provider-to-provider telemedicine, targeted client communication, decision support, digital tracking and digital training of health workers. A table defines each intervention with its synonyms and descriptors. The section also sets out the health areas and outcomes considered for each intervention. It notes that the reviews required a mobile component but that the recommendations may also apply to non-mobile devices such as desktop computers.

sections.title: Evidence retrieval

summary.text: Explains that no restrictions were placed on delivery channels and describes the two main types of evidence used: effectiveness studies such as randomised trials and controlled before-and-after studies, and qualitative studies on acceptability, feasibility and implementation. It notes that evidence on resource use and cost-effectiveness came from what the reviews found. An overarching analysis drew together qualitative reviews, an overview of systematic reviews and mixed-methods analyses.

sections.title: Assessment, synthesis and grading of the evidence

summary.text: Describes how risk of bias in effectiveness studies was assessed using Cochrane methods and how qualitative studies were appraised with an adapted Critical Appraisal Skills Programme tool. It also mentions the WEIRD tool for programme data and the use of GRADE for effectiveness evidence. Confidence in qualitative findings was graded with GRADE-CERQual as high, moderate, low or very low by consensus.

sections.title: Roles and responsibilities of contributors

summary.text: Sets out the roles of the groups that guided guideline development, including the WHO steering group drawn from many departments, the technical team of methodologists, the guideline development group and the external review group. It describes how members were chosen for geographical and gender balance. It also explains how declarations of interest were collected and managed, with biographies posted on the WHO website.

sections.extract: The guideline development process was guided by the WHO steering group, the technical team, the GDG, the external review group, and external partners and observers (see Annex 3 for the list of contributors in these main groups). summary.text: Explains how evidence profiles were consolidated into evidence-to-decision frameworks covering effectiveness, acceptability, feasibility, resource use, and gender, equity and rights. Judgements on these criteria guided the guideline development group's decisions.

sections.extract: The technical team supervised and finalized the preparation of the evidence profiles and evidence summaries. These were then consolidated into an evidence-to-decision framework for each guideline question. The evidence-to-decision frameworks (see Web Supplement 1) provided explicit and systematic presentations of the evidence for each question on the following criteria. sections.title: Decision-making and formulation of recommendations

summary.text: Describes how the guideline development group reviewed evidence-to-decision frameworks at a June 2018 meeting and reached recommendations through discussion and voting. It defines the recommendation categories, including recommended, not recommended, recommended only in specific contexts and recommended only in the context of rigorous research. It also explains how members with declared conflicts of interest could join discussions but not vote on the related questions.

summary.text: Explains that recommendations appear in the executive summary, with evidence summaries in Chapter 3, and that relevant existing WHO recommendations are quoted exactly with added remarks where needed.

sections.extract: The recommendations are presented in the executive summary of this guideline. sections.title: Evidence and recommendations

summary.text: Introduces the chapter presenting ten evidence-based recommendations on the prioritised digital health interventions, listing what is given for each: background, evidence, recommendation with justification and implementation considerations. It refers to annexes and web supplements for evidence gaps and evidence-to-decision frameworks.

sections.extract: recommendations This guideline provides ten evidence-based recommendations on the digital health interventions that were prioritized during the scoping process (see sections 2.1 and 2.2). These recommendations are made with the expectation that their implementation is grounded in an understanding of the ecosystem readiness and maturity, as outlined in Chapter 4. sections.title: Cross-cutting acceptability and feasibility findings

summary.text: Summarises cross-cutting qualitative findings on how acceptable and feasible health workers find digital interventions. Factors that may increase acceptability include the chance for health workers to take on new and more senior tasks, while concerns include extra workload and the cost of using personal phones. Feasibility issues such as connectivity, power, training and device costs are also discussed. The section ends with findings on clients, including privacy worries among people with stigmatised conditions.

sections.extract: feasibility findings Most of the digital health interventions in this guideline are targeted at or expected to be used by health workers. The following findings point to factors that influence the acceptability and feasibility of digital interventions used by health workers. sections.title: Accountability coverage: Birth and death notification

summary.text: Covers digital birth and death notification, linking it to the global plan to strengthen civil registration and vital statistics systems and the spread of mobile phones in resource-limited settings. It summarises evidence on effectiveness, acceptability and feasibility, including community sensitivities around stillbirths and maternal deaths and the need for local staffing. WHO recommends digital birth notification only where notifications provide individual-level data and the health or civil registration system can respond. Implementation considerations include data validation, health worker reporting targets and whether registration systems can absorb more notifications.

sections.extract: birth and death notification Background A global scale-up plan for strengthening civil registration and vital statistics (CRVS) systems has been developed by the World Bank and WHO with the goal of achieving “universal civil registration of births, deaths and other vital events, including reporting cause of death, and access to legal proof of registration for all individuals by 2030” (57). A key component of this

sections.title: Availability of commodities: Stock notification and commodity

summary.text: Covers digital stock notification and commodity management, explaining why stock-outs persist, especially in rural areas, and how mobile tools such as text messaging and dashboards can help track supplies. WHO recommends this intervention only where supply chain systems can respond promptly and appropriately to notifications, despite limited evidence on effectiveness. Implementation considerations are listed against the WHO/ITU eHealth strategy toolkit framework.

sections.extract: stock notification and commodity Background The availability of health commodities at point of services is critical to strengthening the quality of care and supporting the pillars of universal health coverage (UHC) (64). Health commodities include health products, and health and medical supplies that may be needed for the provision of health services, including medicines, vaccines, medical supplies such as

sections.title: Client-to-provider telemedicine

summary.text: Covers client-to-provider telemedicine as a way to overcome geographic barriers and uneven distribution of health workers, defining telemedicine and its forms. It summarises evidence on effects, acceptability and feasibility, including access issues for people with hearing impairments or low digital literacy. WHO recommends it only as a complement to face-to-face care in settings able to monitor safety, privacy, traceability, accountability and security for patients, followed by implementation considerations.

sections.extract: Background Despite progress in addressing health workforce shortages, challenges in the equitable access to health workers serves as a major hindrance to achieving the full requirements of effective coverage of human resources for health (70). Geographical inaccessibility and the preference of health workers for working in urban environments are among some of the well-documented reasons for imbalances in the

sections.title: Provider-to-provider telemedicine

summary.text: Covers provider-to-provider telemedicine, which links less skilled health workers with specialists for diagnosis, remote monitoring and case management, either in real time or by store-and-forward exchange. It summarises the evidence on effects, acceptability and feasibility. WHO recommends it where safety, privacy, traceability, accountability and security for patients can be monitored, including procedures for consent, data protection and checking health worker credentials, followed by implementation considerations.

sections.extract: Background Access to qualified health workers with the appropriate competencies, skills and behaviours is an even greater obstacle to improving health outcomes than the availability of health workers (70,71). Geographical inaccessibility and the unequal distribution of health workers also contribute to limitations in the effective coverage of human resources for health (62). sections.title: child and adolescent health

summary.text: Covers the recommendation on targeted client communication in WHO's guideline on digital interventions for health system strengthening, although the block's title refers to child and adolescent health. It defines the intervention as sending health information, reminders and test result notifications to specific people based on their health status or demographics, through channels such as text messages and voice calls. It reviews the evidence on effectiveness and the considerations behind the recommendation. It ends with implementation advice, including negotiating with mobile network operators over communication costs, before the next section on effective coverage.

sections.extract: Background Targeted client communication2 – defined as the transmission of health content or information to a specific audience based on their health status or demographic profile (13) – represents an approach for engaging with individuals to increase their knowledge about health and health- seeking behaviours, about where to find or how to access services, or for helping to retain them within health services when

sections.title: Effective coverage: Health worker decision support

summary.text: Covers the guideline section on decision support tools for health workers, starting from the definition of quality of care and the reasons it is often poor in low- and middle-income countries. It reviews how digital decision support aims to improve health workers' adherence to recommended practice and the evidence and considerations behind the recommendation. It notes that such tools are often integrated with digital health records and points to the section on combining them with digital tracking.

sections.extract: Health worker decision support Background Quality of care, defined as the “degree to which health services for individuals and populations increase the likelihood of desired health outcomes and are consistent with current professional knowledge”, is a foundational component of universal health coverage (76). Quality of care has consistently been documented as suboptimal, particularly across low- and middle-income

sections.title: Multiple points of coverage: Digital tracking of clients’ health status and services combined with decision-support and targeted client communication

summary.text: Covers the guideline section on digital tracking of clients' health status and services combined with decision support and targeted client communication. It explains how digital registers and electronic records reduce the clerical burden of paper systems and support follow-up and continuity of care. It sets out the evidence and conditions for the recommendation, including concerns about privacy and data security. It closes by urging that local policies on digital identity be considered so that programmes do no harm.

sections.extract: digital tracking of clients’ health status and services combined with decision-support and targeted client communication Background The use of paper-based systems in the delivery of health services introduces a clerical burden on health workers. Additionally, the ability for health workers to keep track of clients effectively, and follow up on services, whether within the facility or in the community, is essential

sections.title: to health workers

summary.text: Covers the guideline section on digital provision of training and educational content to health workers, describing eLearning and mobile learning delivered by text messages, apps, games and other channels, especially in remote or low-resource settings. It reviews the evidence and considerations for the recommendation. Implementation advice includes letting health workers store content for later and offering modular material they can tailor to their needs.

sections.extract: Background Broadly defined as the management and provision of educational and training content in digital form for health professionals, electronic learning (eLearning) has emerged as one approach to increasing health workers’ access to training and educational resources (18). More recently, the widespread reach of mobile devices has prompted the use of such technologies to deliver training content to health

sections.title: Implementation considerations

summary.text: Opens the chapter on implementation considerations, noting that digital health shares the general health system challenges of governance, training, infrastructure and supplies, so the wider enabling environment is critical.

sections.extract: considerations Digital health has the potential to help address problems such as distance and access, but still shares many of the underlying challenges faced by health system interventions in general, including poor governance, insufficient training, infrastructural limitations, and poor access to equipment and supplies. These considerations need to be addressed in addition to specific requirements introduced by

sections.title: Linking the recommendations across the health system

summary.text: Explains how the guideline's separate recommendations on digital interventions link together across the health system, serving managers, clients and health workers through stock notification, telemedicine, targeted communication, decision support and mobile learning. A figure maps each recommendation to health system needs such as availability, accessibility and quality.

sections.extract: across the health system While the recommendations included in this guideline are based on distinct digital interventions, they all contribute to the health systems’ needs in different but interlinked ways. For health system managers, the recommendation on digital stock notification aims to drive availability of commodities at the point of services. From the clients’ and patients’ perspectives, this would include

sections.title: Implementation components

summary.text: Sets out the components on which digital health implementations depend: accurate health content, the digital intervention itself, the software and communication channels that deliver it, and the ICT and enabling environment. A figure shows how these components combine.

sections.extract: Digital health implementations rely on a host of factors, and their success is often mediated by issues intrinsic to the design of the implementation, as well as external factors related to the enabling and ICT environment. The implementation of digital health interventions is broadly predicated on the following critical components: i. appropriate and accurate health content and information aligned with

sections.title: Overarching implementation considerations

summary.text: Presents overarching considerations for implementing digital health, stressing fit with local needs, users and the ICT and enabling environment, and referring to the WHO–ITU National eHealth Strategy Toolkit for assessing readiness. A table describes components of the enabling environment such as leadership and governance, strategy and investment, legislation, infrastructure and workforce. It closes with principles for digital development, including designing with users, building for scale and sustainability, using open standards, and addressing privacy and security.

sections.extract: Overarching implementation considerations Implementations need to be made appropriate to the local needs, intended users, and overall ecosystem comprised of the ICT and enabling environment. The National eHealth strategy toolkit produced jointly by WHO and ITU (18) provides useful considerations for assessing the ICT and enabling environment and can be used to help countries in determining their readiness to adopt

sections.title: Future research

summary.text: Introduces the chapter on future research, which covers cross-cutting evidence gaps on effectiveness, cost, gender, equity and rights, plus specific research questions for each intervention.

sections.extract: This chapter on future research highlights crosscutting evidence gaps observed across a range of interventions in relation to effectiveness, resource use and cost-effectiveness, and gender, equity and rights. In addition, specific research questions are provided for each of the interventions, based on the gaps identified through the evidence-to-decision framework and GDG.

sections.title: Overarching research gaps

summary.text: Describes overarching research gaps found during guideline development, where evidence was of low or very low certainty or absent, often owing to poor reporting, small studies and limited settings. It calls for future research on health system process improvements, resource use and equity effects. It also raises questions on implementing interventions faithfully at scale and suggests frameworks such as RE-AIM to structure implementation research.

sections.extract: Overarching research gaps The following sections describe the overarching research priorities identified through this guideline process. These reflect the general areas in which the available evidence was found to be of low or very low certainty or confidence, or where no direct evidence was identified. sections.title: Considerations for the design of future evaluations

summary.text: Lists the guideline group's suggestions for designing future evaluations of digital health interventions, such as alternatives to randomized trials for complex system-level interventions and attention to intermediate outcomes. It also calls for common metrics and tools for assessing effectiveness and cost-effectiveness.

sections.title: Dissemination and implementation of the guideline

summary.text: Describes how WHO will disseminate the digital health guideline in full and condensed versions through regional offices, global digital health networks, regional consultations and webinars. It also mentions an implementation guide that will provide a stepwise process for fitting recommended interventions to local needs and contexts.

sections.extract: of the guideline This guideline will be available in its full version, as well as a condensed form that includes the executive summary, implementation considerations, and future research priorities. sections.title: Updates and living guidelines approach

summary.text: Explains that the guideline will be treated as a living guideline, with new evidence reviewed as it emerges, and that the first update will add targeted client communication for noncommunicable diseases in version 1.1. It notes the need for continuous scanning of the rapidly changing digital health field.

sections.extract: This guideline will be subject to a phased approach that treats them as living guidelines, supporting the review of new evidence for specific questions on digital health interventions. This will ensure that new evidence is brought to the guideline development group (GDG) for review. sections.title: Evidence maps and illustrative research questions

summary.text: Presents evidence maps showing the certainty of effectiveness evidence for each digital health intervention, mostly low or very low, across outcomes for clients and health workers. Separate tables cover client interventions such as targeted client communication, health worker interventions and health system interventions. A further table lists research gaps with illustrative research questions, including cross-cutting gaps on gender, equity and rights. The section ends with WHO's address and the ISBN.
